entities.name: Reginald of Orleans
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Reginald of Orleans (died 1220), an Italian Dominican friar and Catholic priest, stands as a pivotal early associate of Saint Dominic de Guzmán, whose charismatic preaching and profound spiritual influence were instrumental in shaping the nascent Order of Preachers. Though his life was tragically short, spanning only a few years within the Dominican movement, Reginald's fervent dedication and eloquent sermons in Bologna and Paris significantly contributed to the order's rapid initial expansion and its intellectual foundations. His leadership and example attracted numerous scholars and students, particularly at the University of Bologna, helping to establish the Dominicans as a formidable intellectual and spiritual force across Western Europe during the early 13th century.

Originally a dean and canon at the collegiate church of Saint-Aignan in Orléans, Reginald encountered Saint Dominic in Rome in 1218 while suffering from a grave illness. During his convalescence, Dominic ministered to him, and Reginald made a vow to join the new mendicant order should he recover. True to his word, he entered the Dominicans and was sent by Dominic to Bologna in 1219, where his electrifying preaching captivated the academic community. His sermons, characterized by their intellectual rigor and spiritual depth, drew many prominent masters and students from the University of Bologna into the order, including figures like Blessed Jordan of Saxony, Dominic's eventual successor, and Thomas of Cantimpré. Later dispatched to Paris, Reginald continued his influential work, solidifying the Dominican presence at the University of Paris.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Reginald of Orleans played a critical role in establishing the Dominican Order's intellectual foundation by recruiting numerous prominent scholars and students, including the future Master General Jordan of Saxony, from major European universities. His work ensured the order's early growth and scholarly reputation, which profoundly shaped medieval theology and education.
